title: Washed hands (Mark 7:1–13)
hookLine: he challenges traditions used to dodge caring for parents

cards: A new part of Mark, chapters seven to nine, with one question underneath it all: who is this? It opens at a meal.

Some Pharisees and teachers of the law have come up from Jerusalem, and they notice that some of Jesus's disciples are eating without first washing their hands in the ritual way. It's not about germs.

It's about holiness, the careful washing that set apart an ordinary meal as something done before God. They ask Jesus why his followers don't keep it. And his answer is about something much bigger than hands.

teach.b: Mark explains the custom for his readers: the Pharisees, he says, wash their hands carefully before eating, and wash cups and pots too, keeping the tradition of the elders. It was, and is, a beautiful practice.
Observant Jews today still wash their hands with a blessing before eating bread. A fair question.
Jesus answers with the prophet Isaiah, in the old King James Bible: "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me."

Then his real charge: "laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men." And an example. The commandment says honor your father and mother, which included caring for them in old age.
But, he says, you've allowed someone to declare what they own Corban, dedicated to God, and then use that to refuse their parents any help.
A holy word, used as a loophole. Jewish teachers themselves later wrote rules to release vows that hurt parents, so they saw the danger too.
Tradition, in Greek paradosis, means what's handed over, passed from hand to hand. Christians have traditions of their own, and they don't all weigh them the same way.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold sacred Tradition alongside scripture as a way God's word is handed on. Many Protestants give scripture the final word over any tradition.
Read that way, the passage is a warning to anyone with traditions, churches included: a habit meant to bring you closer to God can end up used to dodge the people God asked you to love.

how: Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold sacred Tradition alongside scripture, while many Protestant churches weigh every tradition against scripture; many Christians read this passage as a call to check their own customs against love of God and neighbor.

games.q: you're asked why your followers eat without the ritual handwashing. what does Jesus talk about?
o: people who use a holy word to dodge caring for their parents.
games.why: he quotes Isaiah, then gives the example of Corban: a holy word used as a loophole to refuse help to father and mother.

practice: Think of something you do regularly because it's good: a prayer routine, if you pray, a family ritual, a rule you keep at work.

Ask what it was for, and then, honestly, whether it's ever become a reason to avoid something, or someone. Don't judge yourself, just look; if you pray, you can ask God to keep the heart of it alive in you.

wordCard.voice: Tradition. From the Greek paradosis, what's handed on. A gift, unless it's used to dodge the love it was meant to carry.
